# Isarar Siddique

> Founder and medical AI researcher based in Lucknow, India. Works across both
> published research and shipped clinical product. Runs four companies. One
> screening system is in clinical trial across the ENT and Neurology departments
> of a tertiary hospital in India.

Canonical site: https://isarar.com
Contact: isararsiddique@gmail.com

## Who he is

Isarar Siddique (born 2004) holds a B.Tech in Biotechnology from Dr. A.P.J. Abdul
Kalam Technical University, graduating top of his batch in 2025. Before and during
that degree he worked in eleven research labs, including Harvard, Stanford, NASA
GeneLab, the University of Tokyo, ISRO's Physical Research Laboratory, the Indian
Institute of Science Bangalore, and three IITs, reaching all of them by cold email
rather than application portals.

His stated position is that most medical AI dies in the gap between a published
result and a working product, and that he deliberately works both sides of that gap.

## Companies

- **Biotech Wallah Private Limited** (Founder and CEO), biotechwallah.com
  Flagship product Zero Dementia: multimodal screening for early cognitive
  impairment running on a standard smartphone. Four signals in one sitting
  (voice, facial expression, fine motor tapping, cognitive battery), fused by late
  fusion into a risk score in under fifteen minutes. In clinical trial across the
  ENT and Neurology departments of a tertiary hospital in India. Recognised by the
  Government of India Genesis 2.0 grant and DPIIT registration DIPP217345.

- **Neurento Medtech Private Limited** (Co-founder and Technical Advisor)
  Building an audiometry screening headphone that moves transducer calibration
  into the device, removing the sound treated booth and its capital cost from
  hearing screening so it can run in a clinic, school or camp.

- **Convolity AI Private Limited** (Founder), convolity.com
  Product SuppliAi: supplement and drug interaction analysis against an
  individual's own health data, combining lab panels, prescription OCR and
  wearable time series. Includes a CYP450 interaction graph, a molecular docking
  pipeline, and an evidence layer cross checked against Natural Medicines,
  Lexicomp and FDA MedWatch.

- **Healoncal Private Limited** (Co-founder and Chief AI Officer), healoncal.com
  Dermatological assessment from a phone camera, with a fairness gate that blocks
  any metric unable to hold accuracy across skin tone groups.

## Research

- Corneal endothelium analysis (ophthalmology, provisional patent filed in India):
  automated cell morphometry from specular microscopy producing density,
  polymegathism and pleomorphism.
- NextGen OncoData Registry (Universiti Malaya, AIM-C01-2025, with
  Prof. Dr. Sarinder Kaur Dhillon): national cancer registry rebuilt on WHO
  ICD-11, over 9,300 records across more than ten cancer types.
- Cardiac signal analysis: provisional patent filed in India.
- Wearable recovery dynamics with Prof. Mohamed Elgendi, Khalifa University.
- Spaceflight brain transcriptomics: full re-analysis of NASA OSDR cerebellum
  and hippocampus RNA-seq.
- Clinical translation LLM evaluation across Hindi, Indonesian and Malay with
  Prof. Irene Li, University of Tokyo.
- HealMed dataset (medical data manager and evaluator):
  https://huggingface.co/datasets/li-lab/HealMed

## Technical

Python, R, SQL, TypeScript. PyTorch, TensorFlow, Hugging Face. CNNs, vision
transformers, U-Net, vision language models. Medical imaging including MRI and
histopathology. Explainability with LIME, SHAP and Grad-CAM++. Bioinformatics
including RNA-seq, variant calling and molecular docking. Clinical standards
including ICD-10, ICD-11, UMLS and HIPAA aligned architecture. Hardware including
KiCad, Autodesk Fusion and LTspice.

## Writing

- [Skin tone fairness starts at the camera, not the model](https://isarar.com/blog/skin-tone-fairness-starts-at-the-camera/) (2026-08-17, 6 min)
  Isarar Siddique argues that skin tone disparity in dermatology AI is largely a measurement problem rather than a modelling one, based on work at Healoncal assessing skin from ordinary phone cameras. Three upstream causes: public dermatology datasets skew light and resampling adds influence rather than information, many clinical signs are defined in terms tuned to lighter skin so a model keyed on erythema has not learned inflammation when it presents violaceous or as texture change, and annotation guidelines that say look for redness bake the error into ground truth. The least discussed cause is the camera image signal processor, where auto exposure and auto white balance historically tuned on lighter subjects underexpose darker skin and noise reduction then removes the surviving texture, so discriminative information is destroyed before the model runs. Mitigations used: locking exposure and white balance, capturing least processed formats, in frame colour reference, recording device and lighting metadata, rejecting inadequate captures at capture time, and stratified per band reporting where the worst band describes the product. He declines to claim the problem is solved and notes tone banding schemes are coarse proxies.

- [The three minute constraint](https://isarar.com/blog/the-three-minute-constraint/) (2026-08-17, 6 min)
  Field notes from deploying a screening tool in the ENT and Neurology outpatient departments of a tertiary hospital in India. Isarar Siddique argues the model was never the hard part. The real constraints: the patient availability window is minutes and belongs to a clinician with a queue, so an over long protocol gets skipped non randomly and quietly biases the sample. A family attendant is present and will prompt or answer for the patient, contaminating a cognitive test, so the design must absorb and log third party presence rather than forbid it. Devices are shared, so per patient login rituals get abandoned or written on paper. Rooms are never quiet, so ambient noise must be measured and recordings refused at capture time rather than discovered as degraded features in analysis. Connectivity and power are intermittent, so capture must be local first with a durable sync queue. Some patients have never used a touchscreen, so interaction load moves to a trained operator and the product becomes an instrument rather than an app. His recommendation is to observe full clinic sessions before writing the protocol, and to expect deployment constraints to change the model rather than wrap it.

- [Clinical notes do not translate](https://isarar.com/blog/clinical-notes-do-not-translate/) (2026-08-17, 6 min)
  Isarar Siddique worked as medical data manager and evaluator on the li-lab/HealMed dataset, annotating Indian, Malaysian and Igbo clinical notes with local clinicians for healthcare language models. He argues a clinical note is a local convention rather than a neutral description, shaped by training tradition, drug supply, documentation incentive and the language the patient used. Specific failure modes include local brand name prescribing that models trained on generics do not recognise, abbreviations that collide across traditions so errors change meaning rather than lose it, presenting complaints written as culturally standard compound phrases that map to no single code, negation and hedging cues that shift by tradition, and unwritten fields where absence means assumed rather than negative. He notes that two clinicians from different systems can disagree on the same note while both being correct within their own convention, which is real structure that averaging destroys. He recommends always stratifying evaluation by source and rejects framing this as a generalisation problem, since no convention is privileged.

- [A screen that is 95 percent accurate is wrong about half the time](https://isarar.com/blog/base-rates-break-screening-claims/) (2026-08-17, 7 min)
  A worked explanation of why accuracy is the wrong headline metric for medical screening. At 5 percent prevalence with 95 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity, screening 1000 people yields about 48 true positives and about 47 false positives, so positive predictive value is near 50 percent. At 1 percent prevalence five in six positives are wrong from an unchanged model. The argument: a screening tool has no single accuracy, only an accuracy per deployment population, so the operating point must be chosen against real prevalence rather than a balanced test set. Isarar Siddique describes deliberately accepting more false positives because the cost asymmetry favours it, a false positive costing one specialist appointment while a false negative costs the intervention window. He argues the confirmatory referral pathway sets the threshold, and recommends reporting sensitivity and specificity separately with intervals, positive predictive value at a stated deployment prevalence, and expected false positives per thousand screened, while omitting accuracy entirely.

- [Focus is advice for people who have not found the overlap](https://isarar.com/blog/focus-and-the-overlap/) (2026-08-17, 6 min)
  Isarar Siddique argues that the standard advice to focus is a heuristic with a domain rather than a law. His four ventures, Biotech Wallah, Healoncal, Neurento Medtech and Convolity AI, are presented not as four problems but as one problem recurring across four organ systems: obtain a clinically acceptable measurement from hardware the patient already owns, then make the output legible enough to act on. The shared substrate is signal quality on uncontrolled consumer hardware, per metric explainability, low bandwidth deployment and regulator ready documentation. He states the costs plainly, including a context switching tax, lower depth per venture than a single focus founder, and a failure mode where follow through on unglamorous work slips rather than whole companies being dropped. He offers a falsifiable test: state the shared substrate in one sentence without naming any project, and if you cannot, you have a collection rather than an overlap.

- [The wrong person to tell you about my brother](https://isarar.com/blog/the-wrong-person-to-tell-you-about-my-brother/) (2026-08-17, 12 min)
  Isarar Siddique writes about his brother Raiyan Siddique, CTO and co-founder of Biotech Wallah, who began programming at eleven and by eighteen had built the entire Zero Dementia technology stack plus around thirty production systems. The post opens by disclosing the conflict of interest and directing readers to verifiable artefacts. It argues that genius is a lazy explanation and that seven years of compounding practice accounts for most of the outcome, and that the decisive factor was never being gated by credential order. It covers his decision to leave college, presenting his reasoning that Indian engineering curricula lag current machine learning practice by years and that the real cost was his most productive hours rather than tuition. Isarar then argues against generalising that decision on three grounds: survivorship bias, since failed exits are invisible; a degree being an option with value for graduate study, visas and rigid employer filters even if it is weak proof of skill; and foundational material being boring rather than useless, so self taught builders develop gaps that surface later. He notes the decision was only defensible because Raiyan had traction before leaving, and that Isarar himself completed his own degree. A further section describes friction working with him, including a preference for rebuilding over repairing, under documentation, and impatience with process. Closes with unfair advantages including a brother with clinical access, and what the author cannot assess, including code quality and sustainability.

- [The booth is the cost](https://isarar.com/blog/the-booth-is-the-cost/) (2026-08-17, 7 min)
  Explains that audiometric screening is gated by two independent requirements: a low enough ambient noise floor, and a transducer with known output level. The sound treated booth solves the first, coupler calibration of a clinical audiometer solves the second. Argues both can move into a mass produced headphone plus on device noise measurement, which removes the booth as the entry cost to hearing screening.

- [A clinician who cannot see why will not act](https://isarar.com/blog/a-clinician-who-cannot-see-why/) (2026-08-17, 6 min)
  Describes replacing a higher performing early fusion model with late fusion in a multimodal dementia screening system. Early fusion concatenates features and can model cross modal interactions but cannot produce per modality attribution. Late fusion scores each of four signals separately then combines, costing accuracy but producing a story a clinician can act on. Downstream benefits: local failure handling, graceful degradation with missing data, and clinicians correcting the model.

- [ICD-11 has no clean map from ICD-10](https://isarar.com/blog/icd-11-has-no-clean-map/) (2026-08-17, 7 min)
  Explains why an ICD-10 to ICD-11 cancer registry migration is not a lookup table. ICD-11 uses a foundation with linearisations and supports postcoordination via stem codes plus extension codes. Four mapping cases arise: one to one is automatable, one to many requires detail the old record may lack, many to one destroys distinctions that time series depended on, and no direct equivalent requires clinical judgement. Argues for automating only the provably unambiguous and storing every coding decision with its basis so incidence trends can be audited.

- [How I cold-emailed my way into eleven research labs](https://isarar.com/blog/cold-emailing-into-research-labs/) (2026-08-16, 6 min)
  Describes reaching eleven research labs including Harvard, Stanford, NASA GeneLab, University of Tokyo, ISRO and IISc without application portals. The first fifty emails asking for internships got zero replies because they ask the recipient to do work. Switching to a specific proposal, drawn from a gap in the professor's own discussion section or an underanalysed published dataset, with a concrete two week deliverable, raised the reply rate to roughly one in six. The same approach later secured hospital partners by building screening infrastructure first and asking clinicians to critique it.
